item.title: Industry urges nuclear recognition in COP31's 35-by-35 pledge
item.description: The role that nuclear can play in achieving the COP31 summit's pledge to increase electricity to 35% of energy demand by 2035 should be acknowledged, industry leaders have said, with nuclear construction at a 40-year high.
item.wnn:fullText:
According to World Nuclear Association’s World Nuclear Outlook Report - which was published in full ahead of the climate summit gathering in Turkey - there was 423 GWe of nuclear capacity at the end 2025 and there is currently 88 GWe of new capacity under construction.

There is a widespread goal of at least tripling nuclear energy capacity by 2050 - 39 countries have now signed the declaration which was launched with 22 signatories during COP28. Six have done so since COP30 - Belgium, Brazil, China, Italy, South Africa and Togo.

Director General of World Nuclear Association, Sama Bilbao y León, speaking at COP31, the United Nations Climate Conference, said: "The conversation has moved from whether we triple nuclear capacity to how fast we can deliver it. That depends on decisions made in the next few years: making the most of the existing fleet, completing projects under way, committing to the next ones, unlocking investment, and investing in people and supply chains.

"There is one more ask for COP31. The Presidency's pledge to raise electricity to 35% of final energy demand by 2035 is a welcome ambition, but it does not specifically acknowledge the role nuclear could play. Reactors already under construction will add around 88 GWe by then, including four reactors here in Türkiye, and more will come from reactors due to start construction over the next few years. Clean energy should be treated on equal terms."

At the moment electricity accounts for about 23% of global final energy consumption and to achieve the 35% goal would require a huge amount of new capacity - according to the International Energy Agency it would need an increase of more than 15,000 terawatt-hours in global electricity generation, equivalent to nearly half of today's output, requiring between 3,000 to 5,000 GWe of new generating capacity, depending on the mix of sources and capacity factor.

The draft of the COP31 35-by-35 Global Electrification Pledge, published in September, says that: "Recognising that achieving the goals of the Paris Agreement and keeping 1.5 degrees alive requires accelerated progress across a broad range of technologies and approaches, including in energy efficiency, renewable energy deployment, electrification, emissions abatement and removals, and other technologies and approaches of end uses across transport, buildings and industry … recognising that increasing electricity's share of final energy consumption can complement and reinforce existing efforts to expand renewable energy and improve energy efficiency by translating electricity supply into economy-wide emissions reductions…

"We declare our intent to work collaboratively and expeditiously to pursue the following objective: To increase electricity's share of total final energy consumption, to reach 35% globally by 2035 ('35 by 35'), in line with pathways consistent with keeping 1.5°C alive and complementary to efforts to expand renewable energy and improve energy efficiency."

A letter to COP31 President, and Turkey's Environment Minister, Murat Kurum, coordinated by Nuclear for Climate which was formed by more than 150 associations worldwide, says: "Climate action must serve both the countries reducing emissions from existing energy systems and communities gaining access to electricity for the first time. Nuclear energy can support meeting both needs, supplying reliable, low-emission electricity and heat at scale, while strengthening energy independence and supporting climate prosperity."

It urges: "In line with the Clean Energy Transition and Electrification Priority, and following the Global Stocktake decision calling for accelerating low-emission technologies, including, inter alia, renewables and nuclear, we urge the global community to advance nuclear energy in the implementation of the '35 by 35' Electrification target, as a low-carbon, firm, reliable and affordable source of electricity."

It also calls for the "Climate Implementation Bridge to expressly include nuclear" and calls for "integrating nuclear energy in green industrialisation strategies. It is an enabler of competitive, resilient and low-carbon industrial production, supporting the decarbonisation of hard-to-abate sectors through electricity, heat and hydrogen production."

French environment minister Monique Barbut, speaking at a COP31 event co-hosted by the French government, Comité Stratégique de la Filière Nucléaire and World Nuclear Association highlighting the momentum behind the declaration to triple nuclear capacity by 2050, said: "Here at COP31, the message is clear: the momentum behind the declaration continues to build. France will keep working with its partners to mobilise the finance, cooperation and international support needed to turn this commitment into reality."

Togo's Minister of Mines and Energy Resources, Robert Koffi Messan Eklo, said: "Africa's energy future will be built on ambition, innovation, and clean power. Togo's commitment to nuclear energy is a powerful signal of that future."

The World Nuclear Outlook Report also highlights the importance of extending the lifetimes of existing nuclear capacity, noting that about half of global nuclear capacity will have been operating for between 60 to 80 years by 2050. It says that life extensions of existing capacity are the most cost-effective form of additional low-carbon generation, and will be important, alongside new capacity, to hitting capacity expansion targets.

item.title: Energy crisis reinforces comeback of nuclear power, says IEA
item.description: Unprecedented disruption in the energy world - primarily resulting from the war in the Middle East - is set to reinforce the comeback of nuclear power, according to the International Energy Agency's latest World Energy Outlook, which has revised its forecast for nuclear upwards.
item.wnn:fullText:
"This year's edition arrives at a moment of extraordinary uncertainty," the International Energy Agency (IEA) said. "It comes as the energy market impacts of the Middle East conflict and disruptions to shipping through the Strait of Hormuz have rippled out to all corners of the world. And this is taking place in a broader context of geopolitical strains, trade tensions, rising climate risks, cyberattacks and more."

The IEA says the global energy system has shown "considerable resilience" in the face of cumulative losses of 2.8 billion barrels of oil and 60 billion cubic metres of gas supply from the Gulf, but increasingly it is falling to consumers - and high prices - to absorb the impact as other buffers are run down. Responses to the crisis vary across countries, but there are some common themes: diversification of energy sources and suppliers; a stronger preference for domestically available resources; and a push for faster electrification. It says the biggest beneficiaries from a pivot towards domestic energy resources are set to be renewables - led by solar PV - and nuclear power, all of which see strong growth across the report's scenarios.

"In an echo of the 1970s, the 2026 crisis is set to reinforce the comeback of nuclear power," the IEA says. It notes that, as of mid-year, nearly 90 GW of new nuclear capacity was under construction - the highest level for more than 35 years, and more than 50 countries now have plans or targets for nuclear power, including new technologies such as small modular reactors. 

"Nuclear power generation has been revised upwards compared with the World Energy Outlook 2025, with much of the upside in China and the United States," the IEA said. "Our projections now open up the prospect of nuclear power growing more rapidly than electricity demand, pointing to an increased share in the electricity mix from its current 9%."


Number of nuclear reactor construction starts by calendar half-year, 1950-2026 (Image: IEA)

The World Energy Outlook 2026 considers the usual three exploratory scenarios. The Stated Policies Scenario provides an outlook based on the latest policy settings, including energy, climate and related industrial policies. The Current Policies Scenario considers a snapshot of policies and regulations that are already in place. The Net Zero Emissions by 2050 Scenario describes a pathway to reduce global energy-related carbon dioxide emissions to net-zero by 2050.

This year's World Energy Outlook also includes two new cases – the Additional Response Case and the Low Hormuz Case - that expand the IEA's analysis of the potential implications of the Middle East conflict beyond those captured in the exploratory scenarios. The Additional Response Case is grounded in supply and demand-side actions that are under consideration by governments, even if they are yet to be turned into formal policy proposals, while the Low Hormuz Case asks whether the energy world could manage without transit through the Strait.

Under the Current Policies Scenario, global nuclear generating capacity increases from 420 GWe in 2024, to 583 GWe in 2035 and reaches 825 GWe in 2050 (compared with 728 GWe in 2050 in last year's edition), while in the Stated Policies Scenario capacity increases to 592 GW in 2035 and 886 GW in 2050 (728 GWe in 2050 in last year's outlook). In the Net Zero Emissions by 2050 Scenario, nuclear capacity rises to 734 GW in 2035 and reaches 1,203 GW in 2050 (up from 1,079 GWe in 2050 in last year's edition).

"The current geopolitical and energy security environment could further boost nuclear power, which can diversify energy mixes and reduce exposure to market volatility while supporting reliability in increasingly electrified economies," World Energy Outlook 2026 says. "As part of the response to the 2026 energy crisis, many countries have confirmed or strengthened plans for nuclear power or extended the lifetimes of existing reactors, and some are reconsidering restrictions on nuclear development. In addition, new demand drivers, including electrification, AI and data centres, are strengthening the case for firm power sources such as nuclear."

IEA Executive Director Fatih Birol said: "The Hormuz crisis has delivered a huge shock to the system. While the energy sector and the global economy have shown considerable resilience, the longer the crisis lasts, the deeper the effects will be. And I don't see any credible pathway for the energy world to return to the way it was before.

"This World Energy Outlook looks past the current turmoil to explore the range of energy futures that could emerge from today's upheaval. By providing multiple scenarios - none of which are forecasts - and analysis of unparalleled scope, it can serve as a reference as countries consider their next steps. It also brings into focus the difficult trade-offs they face. In pursuit of greater energy security, countries must take care not to replace one dependency with another. But encouragingly for the future, energy security and energy transitions have never been so closely aligned."

Sama Bilbao y León, World Nuclear Association's Director General, said: “We welcome the IEA World Energy Outlook 2026 and its clear recognition of the essential role of nuclear energy in the global energy system. Nuclear is not a technology making a comeback, but an energy source that has been the backbone of decarbonisation and energy security for decades, providing today around a quarter of the world’s low-carbon electricity and having reached last year a new global record in nuclear generation. What is changing is the recognition of its value, and we are encouraged to see that reflected increasingly clearly in the IEA’s analysis.

“The World Energy Outlook 2026 captures the scale of the opportunity ahead ... turning these projections into reality will require sustained action and close cooperation between governments, industry, financiers and international organisations ... World Nuclear Association is committed to working closely with the IEA, sharing the most comprehensive and up-to-date industry data and insights so that its analysis fully reflects the performance, potential and rapidly evolving reality of nuclear energy.”

item.title: Akkuyu 1 fuel loading 'could start next month'
item.description: Turkey's first nuclear power unit is preparing for hot tests - with Rosatom hoping that successful completion will allow the start of nuclear fuel loading in December.
item.wnn:fullText:
Hot tests see the unit's equipment and safety systems being tested under standard conditions, but using an external power source rather than nuclear fuel.

According to Strana Rosatom, the in-house publication of Rosatom, Russia's state nuclear corporation, its Director General Alexei Likhachev said: "I very much hope that we will pass these tests successfully, and that loading real fuel into the first reactor vessel will begin as early as December, and that Turkey will receive this long-awaited nuclear electricity in January-February."

He was speaking at World Atomic Day at the UN's COP31 climate summit in Turkey.

The report also said he had been discussing potential investors in the project, with the intergovernmental agreement allowing such stakes up to 49% from companies approved by the Turkish government.

Strana Rosatom says that Likhachev said Turkish entities had already expressed an interest, with confidential negotiations taking place. He believes that Turkish investors' participation "will strengthen the project's organisational and financial sustainability".

As the unit gets closer to starting up, it has also hosted a pre-start-up peer review visit by the World Association of Nuclear Operators. This lasted more than two weeks and involved 17 experts from Belarus, Bulgaria, China, Russia, Slovakia and the USA.

Akkuyu NPP said: "The experts reviewed operating documentation, observed personnel at work and conducted plant walkdowns. The assessment covered equipment condition, arrangements for operations and maintenance, organisational structure and personnel training, emergency preparedness and response, fire and radiation protection, and engineering support."

Background

Akkuyu, in the southern Mersin province, is Turkey's first nuclear power plant. Rosatom is building four VVER-1200 reactors, under a so-called BOO (build-own-operate) model. According to the terms of the 2010 Intergovernmental Agreement between the Russian Federation and the Republic of Turkey, the aim was for the commissioning of the first power unit of the nuclear power plant to take place within seven years from receipt of all permits for the construction of the unit.

The licence for the construction of the first unit was issued in 2018, with construction work beginning that year. Nuclear fuel was delivered to the site in April 2023. The aim has been for unit 1 to begin supplying Turkey's energy system by the end of 2026. First concrete was poured for unit 4 in July 2022.

When the 4,800 MWe plant is completed, it is expected to meet about 10% of Turkey's electricity needs.

Turkey has plans for a second nuclear power plant, at Sinop, and has also been in talks with China about plans for a third plant, in the Thrace region in the country's north-west. 

According to a Bloomberg report last week, Turkey's Energy Minister Alparslan Bayraktar said the country was in talks with Canada and South Korea about new nuclear power projects and expected to finalise its partners in the next few months.

On Thursday AtkinsRéalis's Candu Energy Inc and state-owned Türkiye Nükleer Enerji Anonim Şirketi signed a memorandum of agreement which includes a feasibility study for a potential 4.5 GW plant featuring up to six Candu reactors.

The country is also developing plans for small modular reactors, with the aim of adding 5 GWe of capacity by 2050 - which would mean the equivalent of at least 16 individual SMRs.

item.title: Work programme being planned for next year, as Paks II audit continues
item.description: Construction is continuing and a programme for next year is being prepared, Rosatom said, as Hungary's government continues its review of the Paks II nuclear power project.
item.wnn:fullText:
First concrete was poured for the first new unit in February, before the Hungarian elections saw a change of government.

In May, new Hungarian Prime Minister Peter Magyar's government announced a review of "the status of the Paks Nuclear Power Plant's operating life extension and the contracts for the Paks II project, as well as the entire investment process". During the election campaign he had suggested the price agreed for the new units was too high.

According to a report by the official Russian Tass news agency, Attila Sagodi, CEO and chairman of Paks II said: "We're now conducting a formal, thorough audit of the entire project, covering everything from the design, the readiness of the design documentation and the work schedule to the financial, technological and legal aspects. We plan to complete the audit by the end of this year, then see whether we need to look into any issues in more depth or do any additional work."

He said the Hungarian government was gathering the information it needs on the project before they "can make a considered decision and choose the right course" and added that on financing "the question goes beyond whether the government will provide funding. The EPC (engineering, procurement and construction) contract has a complex structure that imposes obligations on all parties, so the government can't simply decide to do things in a way they want to".

Alexei Likhachev, Director General of Russia's state nuclear corporation Rosatom, speaking at World Atomic Day at the UN's COP31 summit in Turkey, said "the Russian side is understanding and willing to provide the necessary clarifications on economic and technological issues", according to a report in the in-house Strana Rosatom publication.

He also stressed that construction is on-going and said the next step would be the approval of the financial and production plans for next year, adding: "We can only move forward with the project at the speed the client allows us."

Background

The Paks plant, 100 kilometres south of Budapest, currently comprises four Russian-supplied VVER-440 pressurised water reactors, which started up between 1982 and 1987. An inter-governmental agreement was signed in early 2014 for Russian enterprises and their international subcontractors to supply two VVER-1200 reactors at Paks as well as a Russian state loan of up to EUR10.0 billion (USD10.5 billion) to finance 80% of the project.

The construction licence application was submitted in July 2020, the licence was issued in August 2022, and a construction timetable was agreed in 2023, with a target to connect the new units to the grid at the beginning of the 2030s. The Hungarian Atomic Energy Authority issued permits in November 2025 for first concrete pouring for the foundation of what will be Paks unit 5, with first concrete being poured in February this year.

The project is the first Russian nuclear energy construction project started in a country while it is a member of the European Union, and is taking place despite sanctions targeting Russia. It was also the first pouring of first concrete for any nuclear energy unit in the European Union since first concrete was poured in the then EU member country, the UK, for Hinkley Point C unit 2 in December 2019.

item.title: Low electricity prices could impact EPR2 programme funding, auditor warns
item.description: EDF could face difficulties funding its planned construction of six EPR2 reactors, France's state audit office, the Cour des Comptes (Court of Auditors) has said.
item.wnn:fullText:
In February 2022, President Emmanuel Macron announced that the time was right for a nuclear renaissance in France, extending the operation of existing nuclear reactors and unveiling a proposed programme for six new EPR2 reactors, with an option for a further eight EPR2 reactors to follow.

The EPR2 reactor is a pressurised water reactor project developed by EDF and Framatome. It meets the general safety objectives of the third generation of reactors. Its aim is to incorporate design, construction and commissioning experience feedback from the EPR reactor, as well as operating experience from the nuclear reactors currently in service.

The first six EPR2 reactors are to be built at Penly, Gravelines and Bugey, all of which are already home to operating nuclear power plants, with construction pencilled in to start in 2027. Each of the three sites will house a pair of EPR2 reactors, starting with Penly, where preparatory works began in 2024. Penly will serve as a pilot and provide a reference for subsequent projects. The cost was originally estimated at EUR51.7 billion (USD56.4 billion), but this was revised to EUR67.4 billion in 2023. In December last year, EDF said its preliminary cost estimate to build the six EPR2 reactors was EUR72.8 billion (USD80.1 billion), at 2020 prices.

In March 2025, France's Nuclear Policy Council confirmed the main principles and parameters of the financing and regulatory framework for the EPR2 programme. The subsidised loan from the State granted to the EPR2 programme for 60% of the total amount of the programme will be financed by the savings fund of the Caisse des Dépôts. The reactors would also benefit from a contract for difference (CfD) with a strike price of no more than EUR100 (in 2024 euros) per MWh. This mechanism is intended to help cover the full production costs incurred by EDF, with the State making payments to the company whenever market prices fall below this level.

In a new report on state support for energy production, the Court of Auditors has now calculated the cost of the project at EUR84 billion at 2025 values.

It added: "At [electricity] prices below EUR70/MWh, EDF's financing requirements for the construction of future EPR2 reactors would increase significantly. This would also constrain the group's ability to fund the programme without additional state contributions - beyond the subsidised loans already announced - a point highlighted by the Court in its recent report on EDF's economic model.

"In unfavourable price scenarios, one option available to the State would be to forgo cash dividends for all or part of the EPR2 construction period. Depending on the scenario, this could affect the trajectory of public finances by as much as EUR65 billion in cumulative terms between 2026 and 2040. As for the contract for difference mechanism, it will have no budgetary impact until the first EPR units are commissioned - which, at the earliest, would be in 2038."

The European Commission launched an in-depth investigation in April into whether France's planned public support for its new nuclear programme was within the European Union's rules on state aid. France says the new nuclear plans aim to increase energy security for France and neighbouring countries, as well as contributing to the EU's decarbonisation targets.
